title: Smacked Cucumber
subtitle: Pai huang gua, crushed cucumber dressed with garlic, vinegar, and chilli
excerpt: Smacking the cucumber breaks its fibres so the dressing soaks straight in, giving a crunchy, lip-tingling result in under ten minutes. The technique is a Sichuan classic found on every cold-dish table. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Pai huang gua (smacked cucumber) originates in Sichuan and appears in Fuchsia Dunlop's Sichuan Cookery (2001) as one of the archetypal liang cai (cold dishes) served at the start of a meal. The technique of smacking rather than slicing cucumbers to create jagged, sauce-catching surfaces is documented across Sichuan, Hunan, and northern Chinese cold-dish traditions.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dress up to 30 minutes ahead. Longer than that and the cucumbers begin to go soft.

content.text: This serves 4 as a starter or side and takes about 10 minutes, no cooking required. The method is the recipe: a flat smack with a rolling pin splits the cucumber along its fibres, creating ragged surfaces that grip the dressing far better than any knife-cut edge could.
Salt the cucumber pieces for 5 minutes after smacking -- this draws out excess water so the dressing is not diluted. Shake or pat them dry, then dress at the last minute. The numbing tingle from the
Sichuan peppercorns
fades quickly, so serve immediately once dressed.
What you need
Method

Place one cucumber on a chopping board. Lay a rolling pin flat across the middle of the cucumber and press down firmly with both hands until the cucumber cracks along its length. Repeat along the whole length, then do the same with the second cucumber. The cucumber should be split but not mashed.
Cut the smacked cucumber into rough 3 cm pieces at an angle, discarding the seed-heavy core if it is watery. Place in a bowl, toss with the salt, and leave for 5 minutes.

While the cucumber rests, make the dressing. Combine the minced garlic, rice vinegar, light soy sauce, and sugar in a small bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves, then add the chilli oil and the toasted sesame oil.
Taste the dressing. It should be sharp, savoury, and slightly sweet. The
rice vinegar
should be clearly present -- add a little more if the dressing tastes flat.
Drain the salted cucumber and shake off any pooled liquid. Pat dry with a clean cloth or paper towel.

Tip the cucumber into the dressing bowl and toss well to coat. Transfer to a serving plate, pour over any dressing left in the bowl, and finish with the ground Sichuan peppercorns and a final drizzle of
chilli oil
. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The dressing is watery and does not cling
items.cause: The cucumber was not salted long enough or not patted dry
items.fix: Salt for the full 5 minutes and squeeze gently to remove excess moisture before dressing.

items.cause: Insufficient vinegar or the sugar masked the acidity
items.fix: Add rice vinegar in 5 ml increments, tasting after each addition. The sharpness should be distinct.

items.cause: Sichuan peppercorns were old or not toasted
items.fix: Toast fresh Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 60 seconds until fragrant, then grind. Old spice loses its hydroxy-alpha-sanshool content rapidly.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Cold dishes (liang cai) arrive at a Chinese table before the main courses, and smacked cucumber is one of the most ubiquitous. In Sichuan restaurants it arrives with the menu -- a palate-opener that sets up the ma la heat to come. The use of
toasted sesame oil
distinguishes the Chinese version from Korean or Japanese cucumber preparations: it is nutty, slightly bitter, and lingers beneath the chilli heat.
